implementation_notes: The language already contains the pattern: std::lock_guard acquires the mutex in its constructor and releases it in its destructor, and destruction is guaranteed on normal return and on stack unwinding, so a named guard is the complete POSA2 Scoped Locking idiom. The class is non-copyable and non-movable, which keeps the guard tied to exactly the scope it was declared in; hand-written guard classes are only justified when a project predates C++11 or must support a non-standard lock interface.
pitfalls: `std::lock_guard<std::mutex>(m);` without a variable name creates a temporary that is destroyed at the end of the full expression - the code compiles, looks locked and is not.
The guard is neither copyable nor movable, so it cannot be returned from a factory or stored; use std::unique_lock when ownership has to move.
Unlocking must happen on the thread that locked: moving a guard across threads (or passing the mutex to another thread) is undefined behaviour.
A throwing destructor path is impossible by design (destructors are noexcept), so an exception thrown while releasing terminates the process.

variants.name: std::unique_lock (C++11, deferred and movable)
variants.implementation_notes: std::unique_lock is the movable, stateful guard: it supports deferred and timed acquisition, explicit lock()/unlock() during the scope and ownership transfer, which is what condition variables need. cv.wait(lock, pred) releases the mutex while waiting and re-acquires it before returning, a shape a plain lock_guard cannot express. Use it when the lock must be released before the scope ends or acquired with a timeout; otherwise the simpler lock_guard is preferable.
pitfalls: A deferred unique_lock that is never locked still counts as a guard object; code paths that skip the lock() call run unprotected with no diagnostic.
unique_lock is movable - a moved-from guard releases nothing, so the lock now belongs to the destination scope.
Condition variables require unique_lock; passing a lock_guard does not compile, and a wait that never re-checks the predicate produces spurious wakeup bugs.

variants.name: std::scoped_lock (C++17, multi-mutex)
variants.implementation_notes: std::scoped_lock is the C++17 variadic guard: it acquires all given mutexes with the same deadlock-avoidance algorithm as std::lock and releases them in reverse order at scope exit, so multi-object critical sections (transfers, swaps, coordinated updates) need neither manual ordering nor nested guards. With one mutex it is equivalent to lock_guard; the multi-mutex form is the reason to prefer it on C++17 and later toolchains.
pitfalls: It is a C++17 feature: with older toolchains use std::lock(a, b) followed by lock_guard(adopt_lock) on each mutex.
All mutexes are acquired before the body runs, so the body cannot shorten the hold time by ordering its work differently.
Passing the same mutex twice is undefined behaviour (self-deadlock); guard against aliasing when the objects come from callers.
It does not support deferred acquisition, condition-variable waits or ownership transfer - use unique_lock for those.
